1420 Catawba Street, Hickory, NC 28601 | Tel: (828) 555-0147 | Fax: (828) 555-0148

CONFIDENTIAL SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT
INFORME CONFIDENCIAL DE EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE

1. IDENTIFYING INFORMATION / INFORMACIÓN DE IDENTIFICACIÓN

Child's Name: Mateo Alejandro Flores Jiménez (called "Teo" at home)
Date of Birth: March 14, 2021
Chronological Age: 4;7
Sex: Male
Primary Language(s): Spanish (home), English and Spanish (school)
Parents/Guardians: Lucía Flores (mother), Ernesto Jiménez (father)
Siblings in Home: Sol Jiménez (age 7), Diego Jiménez (age 2)
Address: 1420 Oak Hollow Drive, Hickory, NC 28601
Parent Phone: (828) 555-0199
Parent Email: lucia.flores88@example.com
Medicaid ID: 987654321B
CDSA Case ID: CDSA-22-04871
Referral Source: Dr. Patricia Owens, Foothills Pediatrics
Service Coordinator: Marisol Peña, Central Piedmont Children's Developmental Services Agency (CDSA)
Evaluator: Carla Méndez, M.S., CCC-SLP, Bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist
Evaluation Dates: September 8, 2026 and September 15, 2026
Report Date: September 22, 2026
Session Times: 9:15 a.m. to 10:45 a.m. on September 8, 2026; 1:00 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. on September 15, 2026
Location of Evaluation: Central Piedmont CDSA satellite office, Morganton, NC

2. REASON FOR REFERRAL / MOTIVO DE LA REFERENCIA

Teo was referred by Dr. Owens following his 4;7 well-child visit, at which the family reported, in Lucía's words, "no se le entiende casi nada cuando habla con gente que no es de la familia" (he can barely be understood by people outside the family). Ernesto added that Teo's teacher, Miss Ana, at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center, had sent home a note asking the family to "please have his speech checked." This evaluation was requested to assess speech sound production and expressive/receptive language in both English and Spanish and to determine eligibility for ongoing services through the CDSA.

3. BACKGROUND INFORMATION / HISTORIA DEL DESARROLLO

3.1 Birth and Medical History / Historia del Nacimiento y Médica

Lucía reported an uncomplicated pregnancy carried to 38 weeks gestation. Teo was born by vaginal delivery at Catawba Valley Medical Center with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at one and five minutes, and a birth weight of 6 lbs 14 oz. No NICU stay was required. Early motor milestones (sitting, walking) were reportedly within normal limits. Lucía stated, "caminó como al año, pero no decía casi nada hasta como los dos años y medio" (he walked around a year, but he said almost nothing until about two and a half). Teo passed his newborn hearing screen and a repeat screen at age 4 through the CDSA showed hearing within normal limits bilaterally. There is no history of chronic ear infections, though Lucía recalled "dos o tres infecciones de oído, nada más" (two or three ear infections, nothing more) between ages 1 and 2. Teo is not currently on any medications and has no known allergies. Vision was last screened at June 2026 and was reported as normal by Dr. Owens.

3.2 Family and Language History / Historia Familiar y del Lenguaje

Teo lives with his parents, Lucía and Ernesto, his older sister Sol, and his younger brother Diego, at their home in Hickory, NC. The family dog, Rocky, is frequently mentioned by Teo during play and conversation. Spanish is the primary language spoken in the home; Lucía and Ernesto both immigrated from near León, Guanajuato, and speak Spanish to the children almost exclusively, though Sol, who attends second grade, often answers in English, a pattern the family calls "Spanglish de los niños" (the kids' Spanglish).

Lucía currently works the overnight shift at the Carolina Fresh Foods poultry processing plant and picks up additional evening hours cleaning offices through Sparkle Clean Services. In her own words, "trabajo en la planta de pollo Carolina Fresh Foods de noche, y los fines de semana limpio oficinas con Sparkle Clean Services" (I work nights at the Carolina Fresh Foods chicken plant, and on weekends I clean offices with Sparkle Clean Services). Before Teo was born, she worked for several years at La Economía store, which she described as "una tiendita donde conocía a todo el mundo" (a little store where I knew everybody). Ernesto is employed full-time with Blue Ridge Construction Company, framing houses in the Hickory area; he described his schedule as "salgo de la casa bien temprano para la compañía de construcción Blue Ridge" (I leave the house very early for the Blue Ridge construction company). On weekends he sometimes helps his cousin at El Rancherito restaurant, and in prior years, before the children were born, he did seasonal harvest work at Green Valley Farm outside Valdese, NC.

Because both parents work long and irregular hours, childcare responsibilities are shared with doña Lupe, a neighbor who has cared for all three children since Sol was an infant. Lucía stated, "doña Lupe es como de la familia; ella los recoge de la escuela y les da de cenar cuando yo trabajo de noche" (doña Lupe is like family; she picks them up from school and feeds them dinner when I work nights). An aunt, tía Rosa, who still lives near León, Guanajuato, video-calls the family most Sundays, and Teo reportedly enjoys "hablando con tía Rosa por el teléfono" (talking with tía Rosa on the phone), though Lucía noted he is shy and often lets Sol do most of the talking during these calls.

3.3 Developmental, Educational, and Prior Service History

Teo has attended Little Sprouts Early Learning Center since January 2024, currently in the Pre-K classroom taught by Miss Ana with support from la maestra Carmen. Both report that Teo is social and eager to participate but is frequently misunderstood by peers. Miss Ana shared a recent classroom example in which Teo asked a classmate, "Jayden, ¿quieres [EW] jugar?" and Jayden did not understand the request until an adult repeated it. Teo was previously seen for a developmental screening at age 2;6 through Smart Start of Burke County, which recommended monitoring but did not result in a referral at that time. He has not previously received speech-language therapy. An occupational therapist, Mr. Tom, briefly consulted on fine motor concerns in spring 2025 but did not identify ongoing OT needs.

4. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES / PROCEDIMIENTOS DE EVALUACIÓN

This bilingual evaluation was conducted entirely by Carla Méndez, M.S., CCC-SLP, who is fluent in both English and Spanish; no interpreter was required. Procedures included:
- Parent interview and case history review, conducted primarily in Spanish with Lucía
- Classroom observation at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center on September 10, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m.
- Oral-motor and hearing screening
- Standardized and criterion-referenced speech and language testing in both English and Spanish
- Spontaneous language sampling and conversational speech sample
- Dynamic assessment of stimulability and cueing response

5. ASSESSMENT RESULTS / RESULTADOS DE LA EVALUACIÓN

5.1 Standardized Test Results

| Measure | Language | Standard Score | Percentile | Range/CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Preschool Language Scales-5 (PLS-5), Auditory Comprehension | English | 79 | 8th percentile | 73-85 |
| PLS-5, Expressive Communication | English | 72 | 3rd percentile | 65-79 |
| Bilingual English-Spanish Assessment (BESA), Morphosyntax | Spanish | 77 | 6th percentile | 70-84 |
| BESA, Semantics | Spanish | 85 | 16th percentile | 78-92 |
| Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3) | English | 68 | 2nd percentile | 62-74 |
| Khan-Lewis Phonological Analysis-3 (KLPA-3) | English | 70 | 2nd percentile | 64-76 |

On the GFTA-3 picture-naming task, the examiner presented the stimulus item sol (sun). When shown the picture, Teo instead pointed to a family photo on the table and exclaimed, "¡Sol, mi hermana!" requiring redirection back to the picture stimulus before he produced the intended target. His eventual articulatory attempt was transcribed as [tol], substituting /t/ for /s/, consistent with the broader pattern of stopping described below.

5.2 Speech Sound Production

Teo presented with a moderate-to-severe phonological disorder affecting intelligibility in both languages. Phonological processes noted across English and Spanish samples included: final consonant deletion (e.g., "ca_" for "cat"), stopping of fricatives (e.g., /s/ → [t], /f/ → [p]), cluster reduction (e.g., "pay" for "play"), and gliding of liquids (e.g., /ɾ/ → [w] in Spanish words such as "ca[w]o" for "carro"). Intelligibility in connected speech was estimated at 30% for unfamiliar listeners and 60% for familiar listeners.

A brief excerpt from the conversational language sample, transcribed using SALT conventions, illustrates these patterns:

C: "el perro [EW] co[w]e" (the dog runs)
E: ¿quién corre?
C: "Rocky y Sol jugaron en el patio" ("Rocky and Sol played in the yard")
E: ¿y qué hace Diego?
C: "Diego e'tá chiquito, no co[w]e"

These samples were judged consistent with a phonological disorder present across both of Teo's languages, rather than a language-specific articulation difference attributable to typical bilingual phonological development.

5.3 Receptive and Expressive Language

In English, Teo demonstrated difficulty following two-step directions without visual support and produced primarily 3-4 word utterances, often omitting grammatical morphemes (e.g., "he go school" for "he goes to school"). In Spanish, similar morphosyntactic difficulty was noted, including inconsistent use of gender agreement and verb conjugation (e.g., "la perro" instead of "el perro"; "yo quiere" instead of "yo quiero"). These error patterns were present across both languages at a rate exceeding what would be expected for a typically developing bilingual child of his age, supporting a primary language impairment rather than a difference attributable to second-language acquisition alone.

During the narrative retell task, Teo produced an 8-utterance story with limited use of connectives and frequent code-switching mid-sentence, such as: "y entonces el dog, I mean el perro, se fue a la casa de Sol." This type of intrasentential code-switching is a typical and expected feature of bilingual language use and was not counted as an error; however, the overall narrative was judged brief and poorly sequenced relative to age expectations in both languages.

5.4 Oral-Motor and Hearing Screening

Oral-motor examination revealed structures and function within normal limits for speech; no evidence of apraxia of speech was observed. A pure-tone hearing screening administered at 9:40 a.m. on September 8, 2026 showed pass bilaterally at 20 dB HL across speech frequencies.

5.5 Stimulability and Response to Cueing

Teo was stimulable for /s/ in isolation with moderate cues (visual and tactile), achieving 8/10 correct productions in a drill task. He was stimulable for /ɾ/ with maximal cues, achieving 3 of 10 correct productions. Final consonants were stimulable with minimal cues in single words (e.g., "cat," "dog") but not maintained in connected speech. This favorable response to cueing suggests good candidacy for direct intervention using a cycles-based approach.

6. CLASSROOM AND HOME OBSERVATIONS

During the classroom observation from 10:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m., Teo was observed attempting to initiate play with a peer, Jayden, and with Camila, both of whom required repetition or adult mediation to understand him. Miss Ana noted that Teo has begun to show frustration, sometimes refusing to repeat himself: "se le nota que se frustra, a veces mejor se queda callado" (you can tell he gets frustrated; sometimes he'd rather just stay quiet). La maestra Carmen echoed this, adding that he is otherwise well liked and plays cooperatively when activities do not require much verbal exchange.

At home, Lucía reported that Teo's daily routine includes waking around 6:45 a.m., arriving at daycare by 7:30 a.m., a rest period from 1:00 p.m. to 2:30 p.m., and being picked up by doña Lupe around 5:00 p.m. on days Lucía works the overnight shift. Evening routines often include Teo playing with Rocky in the backyard and "peleando" (play-fighting) with his brother Diego before dinner around 7:00 p.m..

7. SUMMARY OF FINDINGS / RESUMEN DE HALLAZGOS

Teo presents with a moderate-to-severe phonological disorder and a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder affecting both English and Spanish, consistent with a primary (not language-difference-related) communication disorder. His difficulties are present across both languages in a pattern inconsistent with typical second-language acquisition or typical bilingual phonological variation, supporting true impairment rather than a dialectal or bilingual difference. His strong stimulability and positive response to cueing, along with his social motivation to communicate, are significant strengths that support a favorable prognosis with consistent intervention.

Diagnostic impressions: Phonological disorder (ICD-10: F80.0); Mixed receptive-expressive language disorder (ICD-10: F80.2). Evaluation billed under CPT 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression) and CPT 92506 modifier -59.

8. RECOMMENDATIONS / RECOMENDACIONES

1. Teo is recommended for individual speech-language therapy twice weekly, 30 minutes per session, provided bilingually in English and Spanish where possible.
2. Therapy approach should incorporate a Cycles phonological approach targeting final consonants, fricatives, and liquids across both languages, with Hanen-based strategies ("It Takes Two to Talk") coached to Lucía and Ernesto for use during daily routines.
3. Classroom staff, including Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen, should be given simple strategies (modeling, repetition, expansion) to support Teo during peer interactions with children such as Jayden and Camila.
4. The family, including caregiver doña Lupe, should continue to use Spanish as the home language; there is no indication that reducing Spanish input would benefit Teo's English development, and bilingual exposure should be supported, not discouraged.
5. A referral to Central Piedmont CDSA for IFSP Outcome #2 revision is recommended to formally incorporate these speech-language goals, with review scheduled for March 2027.
6. Re-screening of hearing is recommended at the next well-child visit with Dr. Owens given the history of early ear infections.
7. Follow-up re-evaluation is recommended in approximately 6 months to monitor progress and adjust the plan of care.

9. RESUMEN PARA LA FAMILIA / SUMMARY FOR THE FAMILY

Durante esta evaluación, Teo mostró dificultad para producir ciertos sonidos del habla y para formar oraciones completas, tanto en español como en inglés. Esto no se debe a que esté aprendiendo dos idiomas; de hecho, seguir hablándole en español en casa es bueno para él y debe continuar. Se recomienda terapia del habla y lenguaje dos veces por semana. Lucía and Ernesto are encouraged to continue narrating daily routines aloud to Teo, in either language, and to celebrate his attempts to communicate even when unclear, rather than correcting every error.

This report, and all records related to this evaluation, are maintained as confidential records under applicable state and federal law. Questions regarding this report may be directed to Carla Méndez at Piedmont Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC, (828) 555-0147.

Respectfully submitted,

Carla Méndez, M.S., CCC-SLP
Bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist
Piedmont Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC
Report completed: September 22, 2026

> >
> > REASON FOR REFERRAL
> > Mateo was referred by the Wake County CDSA following concern raised at his 24-month well-child visit regarding limited expressive vocabulary in both English and Spanish. His mother, Lucía, reports, "No nos entiende cuando le pedimos cosas simples, y casi no repite palabras." Javier adds that Mateo "gets frustrated and just points or screams instead of talking."
> >
> > BACKGROUND INFORMATION / Historia del desarrollo
> > Mateo is a 2;2-year-old bilingual (Spanish/English) toddler who lives with his parents, his sister Camila, and his maternal grandmother, Rosa Paredes Gómez, who provides afternoon childcare while Lucía works. The family resides at 412 Juniper Hollow Drive, Garner, NC 27529. Lucía was born and raised in El Rosario, Yoro, Honduras, a small farming village, and moved to North Carolina in 2015; she maintains close contact with family there, and Mateo has not yet traveled to visit. Javier was born in Garner and works for Triangle Freight Logistics as a warehouse supervisor.
> >
> > BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY
> > Mateo was born at 32 weeks gestation at WakeMed Faison Women's Hospital, Raleigh Campus, following preterm labor. Birth weight was 3 lbs, 14 oz (1,756 grams). Apgar scores were 5 at one minute and 7 at five minutes. He spent 26 days in the WakeMed Faison Women's Hospital Neonatal Intensive Care Unit for respiratory support and feeding difficulty, during which Dr. Patel and NICU staff coordinated an early feeding and swallowing consult. He was discharged home at 35 weeks corrected age with no supplemental oxygen.
> >
> > Hearing was screened at birth and passed bilaterally. A follow-up diagnostic audiological evaluation was completed at 18 months by Dr. Daniel Kim at UNC Health Rex Audiology & ENT due to a history of recurrent otitis media (three episodes between 10 and 16 months); results showed normal hearing sensitivity bilaterally with type A tympanograms at that time. No current ear infections per parent report. Lucía notes "se enferma mucho de los oídos cuando hace frío."
> >
> > No history of seizures. Vision screening normal. Mateo takes no current medications. Family history is significant for a maternal cousin with a diagnosed language disorder; Rosa Paredes Gómez reports this cousin, who lives in Honduras, "tardó mucho en hablar también."

> > DEVELOPMENTAL AND LANGUAGE HISTORY
> > Mateo's motor milestones were mildly delayed, consistent with prematurity: he sat independently at 9 months, walked at 19 months. He began attending Little Learners Daycare at 14 months, where his teacher, Ashley Lopez, reports he "plays alongside peers but rarely initiates." A classmate named Dylan reportedly tries to include Mateo in play but Mateo "just watches."

> > Language exposure is mixed: Lucía and Rosa speak primarily Spanish to Mateo; Javier and Camila speak primarily English; Little Learners Daycare is English-only. Per parent report (Bilingual Input-Output Survey), estimated home language input is 60% Spanish, 40% English. Lucía reports first words emerged around 20 months ("mamá," "agua," "no") and that current expressive vocabulary across both languages is estimated at fewer than 20 words. Javier reports Mateo understands simple directions in English "most of the time" but often needs the direction repeated or modeled ("mod cues").

> > Camila, age 5, is reportedly a strong talker in both languages and often "habla por él" (talks for him), per Lucía, which the family was counseled may reduce Mateo's opportunities for independent communication attempts.

> > ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES
> > Assessment was conducted across two sessions at Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC with Carla Reyes interpreting and co-administering Spanish items. Procedures included parent interview, informal play-based observation, standardized testing in English and Spanish, oral-motor examination, and a 20-minute language sample.

TEST RESULTS

Standardized measures administered:

| Measure | Language | Standard Score | Percentile | Age Equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale | English | N/A (criterion-referenced) | — | 11-13 months |
| Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale | Spanish | N/A (criterion-referenced) | — | 12-14 months |
| Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition, Language Composite | English/Spanish combined | 73 | 4th | 12-14 months |
| Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition | Spanish (modified administration) | 68 | 2nd | 14 months |
| Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition | English (emerging sounds only, limited productivity) | Not scored — insufficient verbal output | — | — |

Confidence interval for the Bayley-4 Language Composite: 68-78 (95% CI). Rossetti age range across both languages: 11-14 months.

> > Given limited single-word output, a full Goldman-Fristoe protocol could not be completed; phonetic inventory was derived from spontaneous speech sample instead. Mateo's phonetic inventory includes /m/, /p/, /b/, /n/, /w/ in word-initial position. He was stimulable for /k/ with max cues and produced [k] for "cookie" once during snack. He does not yet produce the Spanish tap /ɾ/; "perro" was approximated as "[peo]." Vowel inventory appears age-appropriate.

> > Language sample (20 minutes, both languages combined) yielded a total of 34 intelligible word attempts, 9 distinct words, and no two-word combinations. Mean length of utterance could not be calculated meaningfully given the single-word stage. One SALT-coded utterance of note: Mateo pointed to his cup and said "[EW] agua" — coded as an early word attempt per SALT conventions.

> > Receptive skills were observed to be stronger than expressive in both languages: Mateo followed 8/10 one-step directions in Spanish with gestural support and 6/10 in English without support. Joint attention and gesture use (pointing, reaching, waving "bye") were judged age-appropriate; pretend play was observed at an early symbolic level (feeding a stuffed animal, pushing a toy car while saying "bu" for "vroom").

> > Oral-motor exam was unremarkable; no structural concerns noted. Feeding history reviewed with parents — no current feeding concerns reported, resolved since NICU discharge per Lucía and prior feeding therapy documentation from WakeMed Faison Women's Hospital.

IMPRESSIONS

Mateo Hernández Cruz presents with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder (ICD-10 F80.2) affecting both Spanish and English, consistent with a true bilingual language delay rather than typical bilingual variation, given delays relative to age expectations in both languages and a significant history of prematurity, NICU stay, and recurrent otitis media. His receptive language in Spanish, his primary home language, is relatively stronger than his receptive English, which is expected given current input patterns; expressive language is significantly delayed in both languages. Phonological development is emerging but limited by overall language level rather than a primary speech sound disorder at this time; this should be re-screened once expressive vocabulary expands.

> > Mateo demonstrates relative strengths in joint attention, gesture use, and early symbolic play, which are positive prognostic indicators. Family engagement is strong; Lucía, Javier, and Rosa Paredes Gómez are all motivated and consistent in their interactions with him, and the home provides rich — if currently split — language input in two languages.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Mateo qualifies for ongoing early intervention services under NC ITP, CDSA File ITP-2024-048891. Recommend speech-language therapy two times weekly, 30 minutes per session, through the Little Learners Program (note: distinct from Little Learners Daycare), beginning October 20, 2026.
2. Therapy should be conducted bilingually or with ongoing interpreter support (Carla Reyes or equivalent) to support both languages rather than English-only intervention, per current best-practice guidance for bilingual language delay.
3. Recommend a parent-coaching model consistent with Hanen "It Takes Two to Talk" principles, coaching both Lucía and Javier on expansion and modeling strategies in their respective home languages.
4. Recommend the classroom staff at Little Learners Daycare, including Ashley Lopez, receive a brief consult on encouraging Mateo's independent communication attempts rather than anticipating his needs.
5. Counsel family, especially Camila, gently, on allowing brief wait time for Mateo to attempt communication before responding for him.
6. Re-screen hearing with Dr. Kim at UNC Health Rex Audiology & ENT if any further ear infections occur this winter.
7. Re-evaluate articulation and phonology formally with Goldman-Fristoe-3 once expressive vocabulary reaches approximately 50 words.
8. Reassess overall language skills in approximately 6 months, or sooner if the IFSP team requests, using Rossetti and Bayley-4 or Preschool Language Scale, Fifth Edition as appropriate for age at that time.

This evaluation was completed in partial fulfillment of CPT 92523. Please contact me with any questions prior to the October 15, 2026 IFSP meeting.

INFORME DE REVISIÓN DEL PLAN INDIVIDUALIZADO DE SERVICIOS PARA LA FAMILIA (IFSP)
Programa de Intervención Temprana del Infante y del Niño Pequeño de Carolina del Norte (NC Infant-Toddler Program)

Niño: Mateo Alejandro Cruz Villanueva
Fecha de nacimiento: 04/09/2023
Número de Medicaid: 784512093K
Número de expediente del CDSA: WY-22871
Fecha de esta revisión: 09/22/2026
Fecha del IFSP inicial: 11/14/2024
Próxima revisión programada: 03/15/2027

1. INFORMACIÓN DE LA FAMILIA

1.1 Datos del niño

Mateo es un niño de 3;5 que reside en 412 Calle Olive Branch, Mount Olive, Condado de Wayne, 28365. Nació a las 37 semanas de gestación, con un peso al nacer de 2,610 gramos y un puntaje de Apgar de 8/9. Fue referido al programa de intervención temprana después de que su pediatra, el Dr. Manuel Suárez, notara un retraso notable en el lenguaje durante su visita de los 18 meses.

1.2 Datos de los padres y cuidadores

La madre de Mateo, Lucía Rodríguez, trabaja de noche en el Hospital Comunitario de Goldsboro, donde es asistente de limpieza en el turno de 11:00 p.m. a 7:00 a.m. El padre, Francisco Cruz Mendoza, a quien la familia llama "Frank", sostiene dos empleos: trabaja de día en la planta avícola Avícola Carolina del Este y, los fines de semana, hace entregas para UPS. Debido a estos horarios, gran parte del cuidado diario de Mateo recae en su abuela materna, Carmen Villanueva, y en la niñera de la familia, Rosa Hernández, quien cuida a Mateo tres tardes a la semana.

1.3 Composición familiar y otros miembros del hogar

Mateo tiene un hermano mayor, Diego, de 7 años, quien asiste a la escuela primaria local y a quien Mateo imita con frecuencia. La familia también convive con sus primos, Ángel y Valentina, durante los fines de semana cuando la tía de Mateo trabaja. El hogar tiene una perra llamada Luna, que Mateo disfruta mucho y a quien intenta llamar diciendo "[awa]" en lugar de "Luna" (nombre dentro de la producción no se marca como KEEP aparte de la cita fonética).

2. COORDINACIÓN DE SERVICIOS Y CDSA

2.1 Oficina del CDSA

Este caso es administrado por el Centro de Servicios para el Desarrollo Infantil del Condado de Wayne (CDSA de Wayne), ubicado en 215 Avenida Ash, Goldsboro, 28501. El teléfono principal de la oficina es (919) 555-0147.

2.2 Coordinadora de servicios

La coordinadora de servicios asignada es J. Ortiz, quien ha trabajado con la familia desde el inicio del IFSP. Se le puede contactar al correo electrónico j.ortiz@acsienc.org o al teléfono (919) 555-0198.

2.3 Agencia de coordinación de servicios

La coordinación de servicios se presta a través de la Agencia de Coordinación de Servicios Infantiles del Este de Carolina del Norte (ACSI-ENC), bajo contrato con el CDSA de Wayne.

3. PREOCUPACIONES Y PRIORIDADES DE LA FAMILIA (EN LAS PALABRAS DE LA FAMILIA)

Durante la reunión de revisión, Lucía expresó: "Lo que más me preocupa es que Mateo no me dice lo que quiere, solo señala o llora. En la guardería dicen que no habla con los demás niños, y yo quiero que pueda jugar y pedir las cosas como su hermano Diego lo hacía a esta edad."

Frank añadió: "Yo trabajo mucho y no estoy en casa de día, pero cuando llego quiero entender qué necesita mi hijo sin que se frustre y me pegue. Eso es lo más importante para mí ahora."

La familia también mencionó como prioridad que Mateo pueda comunicarse con su niñera, Rosa, sin tanta frustración, y que logre nombrar a sus primos, Ángel y Valentina, cuando juega con ellos.

4. RUTINAS DIARIAS DE LA FAMILIA

Mateo se despierta todos los días alrededor de las 6:30 a.m., cuando su abuela Carmen lo prepara para ir al centro de cuidado infantil Pequeños Pasos, ubicado en Calle Center, Mount Olive. Allí pasa el día con su maestra, Ana Gómez, y con sus compañeros de clase, Emily y Josué, con quienes juega en el área de bloques pero rara vez inicia comunicación verbal.

A las 4:00 p.m., Rosa lo recoge y lo lleva a casa, donde juegan con Luna en el patio hasta la hora de la cena, alrededor de las 6:00 p.m.. Lucía duerme durante el día debido a su turno nocturno, por lo que las rutinas de la tarde las maneja principalmente Rosa o Carmen. La hora del baño, hacia las 7:30 p.m., es un momento que la familia identifica como ideal para practicar comunicación, ya que Mateo está más receptivo y juguetón.

Los fines de semana, cuando Frank no trabaja para UPS, la familia visita a los primos Ángel y Valentina, y Mateo disfruta especialmente del tiempo con Diego, quien le enseña palabras nuevas en inglés y español.

5. OTRAS AGENCIAS Y PROGRAMAS INVOLUCRADOS

La familia recibe asistencia nutricional a través de WIC en la oficina de Goldsboro. También han sido referidos al Departamento de Servicios Sociales del Condado de Wayne (DSS de Wayne) para solicitar asistencia de cuidado infantil subsidiado, dado que ambos padres trabajan. La familia participó anteriormente en un programa de Smart Start para visitas domiciliarias de alfabetización temprana, aunque ese servicio concluyó en 06/2025 por falta de disponibilidad de personal.

6. RESUMEN DEL DESARROLLO Y RESULTADOS DE EVALUACIÓN

La evaluación más reciente, realizada el 08/18/2026 por esta terapeuta del habla y lenguaje bilingüe, incluyó la administración del Preschool Language Scales-5 (PLS-5), edición en español. Mateo obtuvo una puntuación estándar de 68 en Comprensión Auditiva (percentil 2, intervalo de confianza 62-74) y una puntuación estándar de 71 en Comunicación Expresiva (percentil 3), con una edad equivalente de 18 meses. También se administró la Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale, donde Mateo logró 6 de 10 ítems esperados para su edad cronológica.

En el área de habla, Mateo presenta un inventario fonético limitado. Produce de forma consistente los sonidos /m/, /p/ y /a/, pero omite consonantes finales y simplifica grupos consonánticos. Al pedirle que nombrara una pelota, dijo "eota" en lugar de "pelota", y al señalar su vaso dijo "[awa]" en lugar de "agua". Con claves máximas logró aproximar "mamá" con mayor precisión.

La evaluación cognitiva, administrada por la psicóloga del equipo, no mostró hallazgos que indicaran un retraso cognitivo generalizado; los resultados fueron consistentes con un perfil de retraso específico del lenguaje.

7. RESULTADOS DEL IFSP Y ESTRATEGIAS

7.1 Resultado 1: Comunicación funcional en el hogar

Mateo usará al menos 10 palabras o aproximaciones de palabras de forma espontánea para pedir objetos y actividades preferidas durante las rutinas del hogar, en el 80% de las oportunidades observadas, según lo reporten Lucía, Frank y Rosa.

Estrategias: Se capacitará a la familia y a Rosa en el uso del modelo Hanen para el desarrollo del lenguaje, enfocándose en la hora del baño y la hora de la comida como momentos naturales de práctica. Se introducirán tableros de comunicación con imágenes bilingües para apoyar las peticiones de Mateo mientras desarrolla el lenguaje verbal.

7.2 Resultado 2: Interacción con compañeros

Mateo iniciará interacciones comunicativas (gestos, palabras o aproximaciones) con sus compañeros de clase, Emily y Josué, durante el juego estructurado en el Pequeños Pasos, en al menos 3 de 5 oportunidades observadas por la maestra, Ana Gómez.

Estrategias: Se coordinará con Ana Gómez para implementar rutinas de juego estructurado basadas en principios de PROMPT, con apoyo visual y modelado de pares. La terapeuta visitará el salón de clase mensualmente para entrenamiento del personal.

7.3 Resultado 3: Articulación de sonidos clave

Mateo producirá los sonidos /k/, /g/ y /s/ en posición inicial de palabra con claves mínimas a moderadas, alcanzando un nivel de precisión del 70% en palabras objetivo durante sesiones estructuradas, documentado mediante codificación [EW] en las muestras de lenguaje registradas.

Estrategias: Se implementará un enfoque de ciclos fonológicos (Cycles) centrado en patrones de sonidos finales y grupos consonánticos iniciales, con práctica domiciliaria guiada para Lucía y Carmen, dado que son quienes pasan más tiempo con Mateo durante el día.

8. FECHAS Y FRECUENCIA DE SERVICIOS

Terapia de habla y lenguaje: dos sesiones individuales de 50 minutos por semana, en el hogar, a partir del 10/01/2026.

Visitas de consulta en el centro de cuidado infantil: una vez al mes, a partir del 10/15/2026, coordinadas con Ana Gómez en Pequeños Pasos.

Revisión de progreso con la coordinadora de servicios J. Ortiz: trimestral, próxima revisión el 12/18/2026.

Revisión completa del IFSP: programada para el 03/15/2027, según lo exige el reglamento del CDSA de Wayne.

---

REASON FOR REFERRAL / MOTIVO DE LA REFERENCIA

Mateo is a 3;10 year old boy referred by Dr. Patel and by service coordinator Marta Jiménez of Piedmont CDSA for a comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation. His mother, Daniela, reports that "Mateo no habla casi nada todavía, solo unas pocas palabras" ("Mateo barely talks yet, just a few words"). Carlos adds, "He understands a lot, pero no nos dice lo que quiere." The family is bilingual, and both English and Spanish are used at home and in the extended family network.

---

BACKGROUND INFORMATION / INFORMACIÓN DE ANTECEDENTES

Mateo lives with his parents, Daniela del Río and Carlos Ortiz, and his older sister, Camila Ortiz-Vega (age 7;2), at the address listed above. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Benítez, lives nearby and cares for Mateo "dos o tres días a la semana" (two or three days a week) when his parents are at work. The family also has a babysitter, Yolanda Cruz, who helps on weekends. The family's dog, Toby, is described by Camila as "Mateo's best friend," and Rosa reports that Mateo "le habla más al perro que a nosotros" (talks to the dog more than to us).

Daniela works at Blue Ridge Textiles in Hillsborough, and Carlos works construction with variable hours, sometimes for a crew supervised by a family friend, Mr. Alvarado, a neighbor who occasionally watches Mateo when both parents work late. Mateo attends Rayitos de Sol Early Learning three days a week, [X] Monday [X] Wednesday [X] Friday [ ] Tuesday [ ] Thursday, from 8:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.. His lead teacher there, Miss Figueroa, and the assistant teacher, Mr. Thompson-Reyes, both report concerns about Mateo's limited verbal output compared to classmates, including his friend Diego, who is "hablando en oraciones completas" (talking in complete sentences) at the same age, and a classmate, Sofía, with whom Mateo plays well nonverbally during centers.

---

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY / HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO Y MÉDICA

Daniela reports an uncomplicated pregnancy with routine prenatal care, no gestational diabetes, and no substance exposure. Mateo was born at 39 weeks gestation at Piedmont Valley Medical Center on 14 de abril de 2021, via [X] vaginal delivery [ ] C-section. Birth weight was 7 lbs 4 oz, and Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes. No NICU stay was required.

Developmental milestones per parent report:
Sat independently: 6 months
Crawled: 9 months
Walked independently: 13 months
First words: "around 18 months, but he hasn't added many since then" per Carlos

Medical history is significant for recurrent otitis media, with 4 documented episodes between 12 and 24 months of age, treated with antibiotics each time. Mateo had bilateral myringotomy tubes placed on el martes 4 de junio de 2023 by Dr. Nguyen, ENT, at Piedmont Valley Medical Center. A follow-up hearing screening on 07/18/2023 showed hearing within normal limits bilaterally, and tubes have since extruded without complication. No history of seizures, significant illness, or additional hospitalization. Mateo is not currently on any medications. Vision was last screened as normal at his well-child visit on 01/09/2025.

---

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY / HISTORIA FAMILIAR Y DE LENGUAJE

Language exposure in the home / Exposición de idiomas en el hogar:
[X] Spanish spoken by mother  [X] English spoken by father  [X] Spanish spoken by sister  [X] English spoken by sister
[ ] Only Spanish  [ ] Only English  [X] Both languages mixed/code-switched

Daniela reports, "En casa hablamos los dos, pero yo le hablo más en español porque es mi idioma, el idioma de mi mamá también." (At home we speak both, but I speak to him more in Spanish because it's my language, my mother's language too.) Carlos speaks primarily English with Mateo, while Camila code-switches freely, often translating for her brother: "Camila le dice 'dile gracias' y después lo traduce" per Daniela. Rosa speaks only Spanish with Mateo and reports frustration that "él no me contesta, solo señala" (he doesn't answer me, he only points).

There is no family history of speech-language disorders, autism, or learning disabilities reported on the maternal side. On the paternal side, Carlos's brother, Luis Ortiz, reportedly had "problemas para hablar de niño" (speech problems as a child) that resolved by early elementary school without formal therapy.

Mateo was previously seen for a developmental screening at Orange County Smart Start on November 2, 2024, which recommended this full bilingual evaluation. He has not previously received speech-language therapy, PT, or OT.

---

CLASSROOM OBSERVATION / OBSERVACIÓN EN EL SALÓN

This examiner observed Mateo briefly at Rayitos de Sol Early Learning on 02/26/2025 from 9:15 a.m. to 10:00 a.m., during free play and circle time.

Observed behaviors / Conductas observadas:
[X] Parallel play  [ ] Cooperative play  [X] Gestural communication  [ ] Verbal initiations with peers
[X] Followed simple routine cues (sitting, lining up)  [ ] Followed multi-step verbal directions without modeling

During circle time, Miss Figueroa sang songs with gestures that Mateo imitated, though he did not vocalize the lyrics. During free play, Mateo pulled Diego's sleeve to request a toy rather than using words, and Mr. Thompson-Reyes noted that this is typical: "He shows us what he wants, pero casi nunca lo pide con palabras."

---

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES / PROCEDIMIENTOS DE EVALUACIÓN

Assessment was conducted bilingually by this examiner, who is a native Spanish speaker and ASHA-certified bilingual SLP, across two sessions. Standardized assessment, language sampling, parent interview, and informal play-based observation were used. Mateo's mother, Daniela, was present for both sessions and assisted with interpretation of Mateo's spontaneous Spanish utterances when needed.

Tools administered / Instrumentos administrados:
- Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) Spanish
- Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3)
- Language sample (50 utterances) analyzed for MLU and vocabulary diversity
- Oral mechanism examination
- Hearing screening (pass bilaterally, 20 dB at 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz)

---

TEST RESULTS / RESULTADOS DE LAS PRUEBAS

Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish)

Subtest | Standard Score | Percentile | Age Equivalent
Auditory Comprehension | 68 | 2nd percentile | 20 months
Expressive Communication | 62 | 1st percentile | 18 months
Total Language Score | 63 | 1st percentile | 19 months

Confidence interval (95%): 58-68

Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale: Overall functioning at the 18-20 month level across interaction-attachment, pragmatics, gesture, play, language comprehension, and language expression categories. Strongest category was interaction-attachment; weakest was language expression.

Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3): Raw score not calculated due to limited verbal output; informal articulation sample obtained during play across both languages.

Speech sound production noted during the session included substitution patterns consistent with phonological processes typical of a much younger child: final consonant deletion (e.g., "ca" for "/kat/" cat), stopping of fricatives (/t/ for /s/), and reduction of consonant clusters. Mateo was observed to produce approximately 15 consonants in his repertoire, with /k/, /p/, /m/, and /b/ used consistently and /s/, /ɾ/, and consonant blends largely absent. He was heard to say "Toby no" when the dog approached his snack, reflecting early negation but no final consonant.

Expressive vocabulary: Parent report and direct observation estimate a combined (English/Spanish) expressive vocabulary of approximately 35-40 words, including "mamá," "papá," "agua," "more," "up," and animal sounds. He combines two words inconsistently, e.g., "más agua" (more water) and "no quiero," observed 3 of 10 opportunities.

Receptive language: Mateo followed 1-step directions in both languages with 8/10 accuracy and 2-step directions with 2/10 accuracy. He identified 6 of 10 common objects by name and 4 of 10 body parts, in both English and Spanish presentations.

Pragmatics and play: Mateo engaged in functional and early symbolic play (feeding a doll, pushing cars with sound effects). Joint attention was present but brief; eye contact was variable, improving with mod cues. He used pointing and reaching to request but rarely combined gesture with vocalization. Turn-taking during a ball-rolling game was achieved with min cues.

Oral mechanism: Structure and function within normal limits for speech; no concerns for feeding or swallowing per parent report or observation.

---

IMPRESSIONS / IMPRESIONES

Mateo presents with a severe mixed receptive-expressive language delay affecting both Spanish and English, consistent with a primary language impairment rather than a language difference attributable to dual-language exposure, given that delays are present and comparable across both languages. His speech sound system is also significantly delayed relative to chronological age expectations. Mateo's history of recurrent otitis media may have contributed to, but does not fully account for, the magnitude of his current delays, as his most recent hearing screening (07/18/2023) was within normal limits.

Mateo qualifies for early intervention services under the North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program eligibility criteria based on standardized test scores more than 1.5 standard deviations below the mean in two domains (receptive and expressive language).

ICD-10: F80.2 (Mixed receptive-expressive language disorder); F80.0 (Phonological disorder)
CPT codes used this visit: 92523 (speech sound and language evaluation), 92521 (evaluation of speech fluency, not applicable, not billed)

---

RECOMMENDATIONS / RECOMENDACIONES

1. Mateo would benefit from individual bilingual speech-language therapy, [X] 2x/week [ ] 1x/week [ ] 3x/week, 30 minutes per session, focusing on expressive and receptive language, vocabulary growth, and speech sound development in both Spanish and English.

2. This examiner recommends a Hanen-based parent coaching approach, specifically It Takes Two to Talk, to train Daniela and Carlos in strategies to expand Mateo's communication during daily routines, including bath time, mealtime, and play with Camila.

3. Given Mateo's limited intelligibility and motor planning difficulties observed during the session, a trial of PROMPT (Prompts for Restructuring Oral Muscular Phonetic Targets) is recommended to address speech sound production through tactile-kinesthetic cueing.

4. For ongoing phonological error patterns, the Cycles approach to phonological remediation is recommended once therapy begins, targeting phonological processes in a cyclical pattern across both languages.

5. Given Mateo's current reliance on gesture and limited verbal output, introduction of a structured augmentative system such as PECS (Picture Exchange Communication System) may support functional communication while verbal skills develop, to be used alongside, not in place of, verbal language stimulation.

6. If articulation delays persist beyond initial phonological intervention, a shift to Kaufman Speech to Language Protocol cards may be considered to support motor planning for multisyllabic word production.

7. Referral to Piedmont CDSA for IFSP development; this report and recommendations should be incorporated into Mateo's [X] Individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP) [ ] Individualized Education Program (IEP), specifically under Outcome 1 and Outcome 2 of a future plan.

8. Continued bilingual language exposure at home is strongly recommended; there is no evidence to suggest reducing Spanish input would benefit Mateo's English development, and doing so risks language loss and reduced family communication with Rosa and other Spanish-dominant relatives.

9. Coordination with Rayitos de Sol Early Learning staff, including Miss Figueroa and Mr. Thompson-Reyes, is recommended to reinforce communication strategies in the classroom setting, with a shared home-school communication log.

10. Audiological monitoring given history of recurrent otitis media; recommend referral back to Dr. Nguyen if further ear infections occur, and an annual hearing screening otherwise.

11. Re-evaluation recommended in 6 months or at IFSP review, tentatively scheduled for el martes 9 de septiembre de 2025, to monitor progress across both languages.

---

CULTURAL AND LINGUISTIC CONSIDERATIONS / CONSIDERACIONES CULTURALES Y LINGÜÍSTICAS

This evaluation was conducted in accordance with best practice for bilingual assessment, comparing Mateo's skills to typical bilingual development rather than monolingual norms where possible. Daniela and Carlos were reassured that code-switching, observed throughout the session and reported at home, is a normal and healthy feature of bilingual development and is not, in itself, a sign of disorder. Rosa was also included in discussion of strategies, given her significant caregiving role, "porque yo lo cuido casi todos los días."

---

Individualized Family Service Plan — Annual Review

Child: María José Hernández Ruiz, known at home as Majo, was born June 14, 2023. Her Child ID is NC-IT-00482913 and her Medicaid number is 982374651A. The family lives at 1420 Rock Quarry Road, Raleigh, NC 27610. Her mother, Ana Ruiz Delgado, grew up in El Rosario, Intibucá, Honduras, a small village she still describes as "donde todo el mundo se conoce." This review meeting took place on September 22, 2026 at the CDSA of the Triangle office, with Service Coordinator Gabriela Soto present along with both parents. I am Patricia Gómez, SLP-CCC, of Little Steps Therapy Services, and I am the author of this report and Majo's primary speech-language provider since the initial IFSP of November 3, 2025.

María José lives with her mother Ana, her father Carlos Hernández Morales, and her older brother Diego, who is 7 years old. Her maternal grandmother, Rosa Delgado, visits from Honduras twice a year and stayed with the family this past spring to help after Carlos's work hours increased at Triangle Construction Group. Ana works part-time at Valle Verde Poultry Processing on the overnight shift, so on weeknights Majo and Diego are often watched by their neighbor and informal babysitter, Marisol Cabrera, who Ana calls "mi mano derecha." The family's dog, Rocky, is a frequent subject of Majo's spontaneous language; she pointed at him last week and said "Wocky" for his name, approximating the target with a mod cue.

Durante la reunión, los padres compartieron sus preocupaciones principales. Ana dijo: "Queremos que Majo hable más para que la entiendan en la escuela y con su familia aquí y en Honduras." Carlos agregó, in English mixed with Spanish, "She understands everything, pero cuando quiere decir algo largo, se frustra y empieza a llorar." Both parents also raised a new priority: transition planning, since Majo turns three in June 2026 and will need to move from Part C services to the preschool system. They specifically asked whether Majo would qualify for services through Wake County Public School System and expressed hope that she could attend Walnut Creek Elementary School, where Diego is currently a student.

Majo's daily routine centers on mornings at home with Ana before Carlos drops her at Estrellitas Daycare on his way to work. She has been in Ms. Lopez's room there since January 2026, and her teacher reports that Majo plays well alongside classmates Esteban and Valentina during centers time but rarely initiates verbal requests, instead pulling adults by the hand. Breakfast routines include Majo requesting "más" for cereal, typically produced as "ma" with vowel distortion; dinner routines involve family-style meals where Diego often translates for Majo when she gets frustrated. Bath time and bedtime are supported by a picture schedule the family received through Smart Start of Wake County, and Ana reports that Majo now points to four of six pictures independently, up from one of six at the last review.

The family also receives support from WIC for nutrition and from DSS for a housing subsidy application currently in process. Importantly, the family was recently connected to the Programa de Apoyo y Recursos para Familias Latinas de Carolina del Norte (PARFLA-NC), a nonprofit that provides bilingual case management and parent training. Ana attended her first PARFLA workshop on August 15, 2026 and reported it was "la primera vez que alguien me explicó todo esto en español, de principio a fin." The family's pediatrician, Dr. Michael Osei, continues to monitor Majo's recurrent ear infections, which the team believes may be contributing to fluctuating hearing and delayed sound development; a referral to audiology was repeated at this visit.

Assessment update: I re-administered the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) in both English and Spanish, with interpretation support from Soledad Reyes, a certified medical interpreter. Majo's Auditory Comprehension standard score was 78 (7th percentile), and her Expressive Communication standard score was 71 (3rd percentile), both administered at a corrected age of 2;9. Her age-equivalent range for expressive skills fell between 18-21 months. On a 20-item parent vocabulary checklist completed by Ana and Carlos together, Majo was reported to produce 34 of 50 target words across both languages, roughly 68%. Articulation screening noted consistent substitution of /k/ with [t] and omission of final consonants, consistent with a phonological process pattern rather than a structural concern. Majo's oral mechanism exam was within normal limits, and her Apgar scores at birth, per the record, were 8 and 9.

Current functional communication: Majo combines two words inconsistently ("mas agua," "no quiero") and uses approximately 15 single words across both languages with moderate cues. She imitates animal sounds readily and will approximate "guau guau" for a dog's bark independent of cueing. She shows strong nonverbal communication, including pointing, showing, and giving, and demonstrates joint attention consistently during shared book reading, particularly with bilingual board books Ana borrows from the CDSA of the Triangle lending library.

Outcomes and Strategies

Outcome 1: María José will use two- to three-word combinations in Spanish and/or English to request desired items and actions across home and daycare settings, increasing from current baseline to 10 spontaneous combinations per 30-minute observation, by March 2027. Strategies: weekly direct SLP sessions using Hanen "It Takes Two to Talk" coaching with Ana and Carlos; modeling expansion in both languages; coaching Ms. Lopez at Estrellitas Daycare on wait-time and forced-choice strategies during snack and centers.

Outcome 2: Majo will increase intelligibility of final consonants in single words to 70% accuracy across three consecutive sessions, measured via spontaneous speech sample and SALT coding ([EW] marked for word-final errors), by March 2027. Strategies: auditory bombardment, minimal pairs targeting /k/ versus /t/, and home practice embedded in bath and bedtime routines, reviewed monthly with Ana via phone.

Outcome 3: The family will understand and access the preschool transition process, including eligibility evaluation through Wake County Public School System and possible placement at Walnut Creek Elementary School, by Majo's third birthday. Strategies: Service Coordinator Gabriela Soto will schedule the transition conference for February 2027; PARFLA case manager Lucía Ventura will accompany the family to the eligibility meeting and provide translation of written materials; the team will share present levels of performance, including today's PLS-5 scores, with the school evaluation team in advance.

Outcome 4: Majo will tolerate novel foods and reduce mealtime refusal behaviors, per parent report, from refusing 6 of 10 presented foods to refusing no more than 2 of 10, by June 2027. This outcome reflects feeding concerns Carlos raised, noting Majo gags on textured foods her brother Diego ate easily at the same age. Strategies: referral to the CDSA's contracted feeding specialist, Rebecca Tran, OT, for a joint evaluation; food chaining strategies introduced at home starting with foods similar to accepted purées.

Administrative notes: Majo's current service authorization runs from November 3, 2025 through November 2, 2026, and this annual review updates outcomes effective September 22, 2026. Direct SLP services continue at one 45-minute session weekly, typically scheduled for 9:30 a.m. on Tuesdays at the family's home, with monthly consultation visits to Estrellitas Daycare scheduled around 2:00 p.m. to observe Majo in Ms. Lopez's room. Billing is submitted under CPT 92507 for individual treatment and CPT 92523 for the annual speech-language evaluation, with diagnosis code ICD-10 F80.9. The family may be reached at (919) 555-0142, and Ana asked that written summaries also go to her email, anaruizdelgado82@gmail.com, so she can share them with Rosa in Honduras.

Next steps include scheduling the audiology referral through CDSA of the Triangle, confirming the Wake County Public School System transition conference date with Gabriela Soto, and following up with PARFLA regarding a parent support group that meets monthly at their office. Ana and Carlos both signed consent for continued services and for release of information between Patricia Gómez, Dr. Michael Osei, and the Wake County Public School System evaluation team. The next annual review is scheduled for September 2027, with a transition-specific check-in planned for February 2027. Ana closed the meeting by saying, "Gracias por explicarnos todo con tanta paciencia — nos ayuda mucho saber qué sigue para Majo."

CAROLINA PEDIATRIC SPEECH & LANGUAGE SERVICES, PLLC
4820 Six Forks Road, Suite 210, Raleigh, NC 27609
Phone: (919) 555-0148 | Fax: (919) 555-0149

CONFIDENTIAL SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Child's Name: María José Fernández Castillo
Date of Birth: March 3, 2022
Chronological Age: 4;7
Gender: Female
Primary Language(s): Spanish and English (simultaneous bilingual)
Dominant Home Language: Spanish
Dates of Evaluation: September 15, 2026 and September 22, 2026
Date of Report: September 29, 2026
Case/Record ID: LD-20394 (LD-20394)
Medicaid ID: 804512976A

Referral Source: Wake County CDSA, Service Coordinator Denise Holt
Examiner: Sarah Whitmore, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual clinician
Interpreter: Rosa Martínez, Spanish Language Interpreter (session 1 only; examiner is bilingual and conducted session 2 directly in Spanish)

PARENT/GUARDIAN INFORMATION

Mother: Lucía Castillo Ramírez
Father: Javier Fernández Soto
Home Address: 118 Pinehollow Court, Garner, NC 27529
Home Phone: (919) 555-0392
Mother's Cell: (919) 555-0417
Email: lucia.castilloramirez@gmail.com
Sibling: Mateo Fernández Castillo, 7-year-old brother, no known speech/language concerns

Other Providers Involved: Dr. Angela Whitfield, pediatrician, Triangle Pediatric Associates; Kelly Nguyen, OTR/L, occupational therapist; Brian Sutter, PT, DPT, physical therapist

REASON FOR REFERRAL

María José was referred by Wake County CDSA for a comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation following concerns raised by her mother, Lucía Castillo Ramírez, and her preschool teacher, Ms. Lopez, regarding limited expressive vocabulary, difficulty following multi-step directions, and reduced intelligibility in both Spanish and English. María José currently attends Forest Pines Elementary School in the Wake County Public School System's pre-kindergarten program, in Ms. Lopez's room.

BACKGROUND AND BIRTH/MEDICAL HISTORY

María José was born at full term, 39 weeks gestational age, via scheduled cesarean section, with a birth weight of 6 lbs 11 oz. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes, respectively. Prenatal course was reportedly unremarkable; mother denies maternal illness, substance use, or complications during pregnancy. María José remained in the hospital nursery for routine monitoring and was discharged home on day two of life.

Medical history is significant for recurrent otitis media, with 4 documented episodes between 8 months and 26 months of age, treated with antibiotics; tympanostomy tubes were placed at 2;3 by an ENT at a children's hospital in Chapel Hill. Most recent audiological evaluation (June 10, 2026) indicated normal hearing bilaterally, within normal limits for pure-tone thresholds, with tubes still in place and functioning. No history of seizures, head trauma, or significant illness. Vision screening is reportedly within normal limits per the pediatrician, Dr. Angela Whitfield.

Developmental milestones: rolled over at 5 months, sat independently at 7 months, walked independently at 14 months. First words (Spanish) reportedly emerged around 16-18 months, with a marked plateau noted by the family between 2;0 and 2;6. Two-word combinations did not reliably emerge until approximately 3;2. Parents report María José was previously enrolled at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center from 18 months through 3;0 before transitioning to the pre-k program at Forest Pines Elementary School.

Living situation and primary caregivers:
[X] Home  [ ] Daycare (after school)
[X] Lives with both biological parents
[ ] Lives with grandparent(s)
[X] Sibling(s) in home: Mateo
[ ] Other relative caregiver

María José's maternal grandmother, Rosario Castillo, provides after-school care on Tuesdays and Thursdays while both parents are at work. Father, Javier Fernández Soto, is employed full-time at Caterpillar Inc.'s distribution facility in Clayton, NC. Mother, Lucía Castillo Ramírez, works part-time as a home health aide and manages the majority of daytime caregiving.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

The family's primary home language is Spanish (Mexican dialect, with regional vocabulary from the state of Guanajuato, where both parents were raised). Mother reports approximately 80% of input and output at home is in Spanish, with English introduced primarily through María José's older brother, Mateo, and through pre-k attendance since 3;0. Parents deny any family history of speech, language, or learning disorders, though mother notes a maternal uncle was "late to talk" as a child with no formal diagnosis.

The family received WIC nutritional support through WIC until María José turned 5, and Early Intervention services were coordinated through Wake County CDSA beginning at 2;9 following parental concern about limited vocabulary. An Individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP) was developed on January 14, 2025, with the most recent review conducted on July 22, 2026. IFSP Outcome 2, targeting expansion of expressive vocabulary across both languages, remains active and is the primary focus of current services.

CLASSROOM AND SCHOOL OBSERVATIONS

Per teacher report, Ms. Lopez of Forest Pines Elementary School describes María José as social and eager to interact with peers but often relies on gesture and pointing when verbal communication breaks down. During a brief classroom observation on September 17, 2026, María José was observed attempting to initiate play with a classmate, Jaylen, using primarily single words and gesture; the interaction was successful but brief. A classroom aide, Mrs. Oduya, reported similar observations of reduced spontaneous language use compared to same-age peers.

Educational placement:
[X] General education pre-k classroom
[ ] Self-contained classroom
[X] Receives Speech-Language services at school (1x/week, 30 min)
[ ] Receives OT services at school
[X] Receives OT services through CDSA (home-based)

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

The following standardized and informal measures were administered across two sessions, using Spanish and English materials as appropriate, with support from interpreter Rosa Martínez for session 1:

- Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition - Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish)
- Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fifth Edition (CELF-5)
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)
- Oral-motor examination
- Language sample analysis (Spanish and English, SALT coded)
- Parent interview and case history review
- Informal bilingual vocabulary checklist

TEST RESULTS

| Test/Subtest | Date | Standard Score | 95% CI | Percentile |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension | 09/15/2026 | 73 | 68-78 | 4th |
| PLS-5 Expressive Communication | 09/15/2026 | 79 | 72-86 | 8th |
| PLS-5 Total Language Score | 09/15/2026 | 74 | 69-79 | 4th |
| CELF-5 Core Language Score | 09/22/2026 | 71 | 65-77 | 3rd |
| CELF-5 Receptive Language Index | 09/22/2026 | 76 | 70-82 | 5th |
| GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words | 09/22/2026 | 81 | 76-86 | 10th |

ORAL MECHANISM EXAMINATION

Oral structures appeared symmetrical with adequate range of motion for lips, tongue, and jaw. No overt signs of oral-motor weakness or dysarthria noted. Dentition age-appropriate. Hard and soft palate intact, no evidence of submucous cleft. Diadochokinetic rates were mildly reduced for age but within functional limits for connected speech.

SPEECH SOUND PRODUCTION

In single-word and connected-speech sampling across both languages, María José demonstrated the following error patterns: fronting of /k/ and /g/ (e.g., "tapo" for "capo"), gliding of /r/ and the Spanish tap /ɾ/ (e.g., "uata" for "rata"), and final consonant deletion in English multisyllabic words. Overall speech intelligibility was estimated at approximately 60-70% to unfamiliar listeners in connected speech, improving to 85% in structured single-word tasks with min-mod cues. These error patterns were consistent across both Spanish and English, supporting a true phonological disorder rather than a dialectal or second-language difference, per bilingual scoring guidelines.

LANGUAGE SAMPLE AND PRAGMATICS

A 50-utterance spontaneous language sample was collected in Spanish and coded using SALT, including instances of [EW] codes for word-level errors. Mean length of utterance was below age expectations, with frequent omission of grammatical morphemes (plural markers, verb conjugations) in both languages. María José used primarily 2-3 word utterances, with occasional 4-word combinations. She demonstrated appropriate eye contact, turn-taking, and joint attention during structured and semi-structured tasks, and responded to her name consistently. No concerns regarding social communication or pragmatic skills were noted by examiner or parent.

RECEPTIVE AND EXPRESSIVE VOCABULARY

Informal bilingual vocabulary screening suggested a combined (conceptual) vocabulary within low-average range when both languages were considered together, though each language in isolation fell below age expectations. This pattern is consistent with typical bilingual development but was judged, in combination with standardized scores and parent/teacher report, to reflect a true underlying language disorder rather than solely a bilingual language-learning difference.

IMPRESSIONS

Based on standardized testing, language sampling, parent and teacher report, and classroom observation, María José presents with a Mixed Receptive-Expressive Language Disorder (F80.2) affecting both Spanish and English, along with a co-occurring Speech Sound Disorder (F80.0) characterized by phonological error patterns present in both languages. Findings are consistent across formal testing, informal sampling, and functional report from multiple sources (parent, teacher, examiner), supporting the diagnostic impression that these difficulties reflect a true disorder rather than typical second-language acquisition or dialectal variation.

Strengths noted include strong social engagement, appropriate pragmatic skills, intact hearing (with tubes in place), and a supportive, language-rich bilingual home environment. Areas of concern include reduced intelligibility, limited expressive vocabulary in both languages, morphosyntactic difficulties, and below-average receptive and expressive language scores.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. María José qualifies for ongoing speech-language intervention services. Recommend increasing frequency from current 1x/week school-based services to 2x/week, 30 minutes individual sessions, provided bilingually or with interpreter support as needed.
2. Continue coordination with Wake County CDSA regarding IFSP Outcome 2 and consider adding a new outcome targeting speech sound production.
3. Implement a PROMPT-informed approach to address phonological error patterns, alongside a Hanen-based parent coaching model to support expressive vocabulary growth across both languages at home.
4. Recommend continued collaboration with occupational therapist Kelly Nguyen and physical therapist Brian Sutter regarding any fine- or gross-motor factors affecting oral-motor coordination or classroom participation.
5. Share results with classroom teacher, Ms. Lopez, and classroom aide, Mrs. Oduya, to support classroom-based language facilitation strategies.
6. Recommend repeat audiological monitoring given history of recurrent otitis media and tympanostomy tubes; coordinate with pediatrician Dr. Angela Whitfield regarding tube status at next well-child visit.
7. Encourage continued rich language exposure in Spanish at home with support from extended family, including grandmother Rosario Castillo, while maintaining English exposure through school and sibling interaction.
8. Re-evaluate in 6 months to monitor progress and adjust IFSP goals as needed; next review anticipated January 20, 2027.

Billing codes for today's services: 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression), 92522 (evaluation of speech sound production).

This report was prepared following direct assessment, parent interview, interpreter-supported session 1 (Rosa Martínez), and review of prior CDSA and medical records. Please contact this office with any questions.

Family concerns and priorities, in the family's own words:

+ CA: 4;2
+ Context: Home-based teletherapy session, 3:30 PM, parent Rosa Flores present

Mateo presented well-rested for today's 45-minute session following his follow-up ENT visit at UNC Health Rex Audiology, Cary Campus on October 6, 2026. Tympanometry results were reviewed with Dr. Hannah Kim; bilateral pressure equalization tubes remain patent. Articulation probe targeting velar fronting continued using Cycles phonological approach, cycle 3 of Hanen-informed home program. Mateo produced /k/ in isolation with min cues (target word "cat" → "tat" → "kat", 8/10 trials), generalizing to connected speech at 3 of 5 opportunities.

Joint attention activities incorporated PECS exchange for requesting, with Chispa (family dog) used as motivating stimulus — Mateo exchanged icon independently, saying "go Chispa". Expressive vocabulary growth noted per PLS-5 rescreen, standard score 82 (73-91 CI), up from baseline.

Mother reports continued support from babysitter Dayana Ortiz, who reinforces PROMPT tactile cues during play. Classmates Liam Chen and Ava Patterson from his preschool group at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center joined briefly via video for a turn-taking activity, prompting spontaneous two-word combinations.

Family recently relocated from Vereda San Isidro, near Copán, Honduras, to 412 Willowbrook Lane, Cary, NC 27511. Cousin Esteban Reyes still resides in San Isidro and video-calls weekly, supporting Spanish maintenance. Mother works at Cary Toyota.

Plan: continue Cycles approach targeting /k/, /g/; introduce Kaufman praxis cards next session; coordinate with CDSA of the Triangle service coordinator Grace Thompson regarding IFSP outcome 2 progress review on November 3, 2026. — Sarah Jennings, M.S., CCC-SLP, Carolina Pediatric Speech Partners
